findings.quote:
Medicaid and the ACA are not the same thing. The Affordable Care Act (ACA) is a law, and [Medicaid](https://www.healthcare.gov/medicaid-chip/getting-medicaid-chip/) is a joint federal and state public coverage program. Marketplace plans are private health insurance. In an ACA vs Medicaid comparison, Marketplace plans are bought through the [Health Insurance Marketplace](https://www.healthcare.gov/quick-guide/one-page-guide-to-the-marketplace/). States run Medicaid within federal guidelines. [HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/medicaid-limited-benefits/) states that a person in a Medicaid program that counts as minimum essential coverage is not eligible for a premium tax credit or other savings on a Marketplace plan.

Limited-benefit Medicaid that does not count as minimum essential coverage may still allow those savings. A 2027 Medicaid work-requirement denial can also leave some adults with Marketplace access but no savings. The Marketplace or the state Medicaid agency makes the eligibility decision for each person in a household.
findings.replacement:
The [Affordable Care Act (ACA)](https://www.nyc.gov/site/ochia/your-rights/affordable-care-act.page) is a law, while [Medicaid](https://www.healthcare.gov/medicaid-chip/getting-medicaid-chip/) is a public coverage program. ACA vs Medicaid compares private [Marketplace plans](https://www.healthcare.gov/quick-guide/one-page-guide-to-the-marketplace/) with joint federal-state Medicaid coverage.

States run Medicaid within federal guidelines. [HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/medicaid-limited-benefits/) says full-benefit Medicaid generally prevents Marketplace premium savings. Limited-benefit Medicaid that does not count as minimum essential coverage may still allow those savings.

A 2027 Medicaid work-requirement denial can also leave some adults with Marketplace access but no savings. The Marketplace or state Medicaid agency makes the eligibility decision for each person in a household.

findings.field: ACA vs Medicaid Eligibility and Savings
findings.quote: A person eligible for full Medicaid or CHIP who keeps a Marketplace plan pays full price for the premium and for covered services.
findings.replacement: A person eligible for full Medicaid or CHIP who keeps a Marketplace plan generally pays full price for the premium and for covered services.
findings.defect: Qualify the general rule to agree with the explicitly explained IRS initial-assessment timing exception.

findings.quote: A person eligible for full-benefit Medicaid gets free or low-cost coverage there, and would pay full price for a Marketplace plan.
findings.replacement: A person eligible for full-benefit Medicaid gets free or low-cost coverage there, and would generally pay full price for a Marketplace plan.
findings.defect: Same general-rule qualification; do not imply the detailed IRS timing exception is impossible.

findings.field: Can you have Medicaid and Marketplace insurance at the same time?
findings.quote: Yes, a person can keep both, but full-benefit Medicaid means paying full price for the Marketplace plan premium and covered services.
findings.replacement: Yes, a person can keep both, but full-benefit Medicaid generally means paying full price for the Marketplace plan premium and covered services.
findings.defect: Same general-rule qualification in the FAQ; limited-benefit and timing explanations remain intact.

findings.quote: If income changes month to month, [budget insurance with irregular income](/guides/how-to-budget-with-irregular-income/) before you update the Marketplace income estimate.
findings.replacement: If income changes month to month, [budget insurance with irregular income](/guides/how-to-budget-with-irregular-income/). [Update your Marketplace income estimate](https://www.healthcare.gov/income-and-household-information/income/) whenever expected income changes, then check how that affects your ACA vs Medicaid coverage.
